newsitem.title: USA: Rockwell holders approve unit sale to Boeing.
newsitem.headline: Rockwell holders approve unit sale to Boeing.

text.p: Rockwell International Corp said Wedneday that 97 percent of its shareholders had approved the sale of the company's aerospace and defense businesses to Boeing Co.
Rockwell shareholders will receive 0.042 share of Boeing for each Rockwell share held, the company said.
Boeing will also assume about $2.2 billion of Rockwell debt and retiree liability, leaving Rockwell essentially debt free, the company said.
Boeing will issue about 9.19 million shares in the deal, Rockwell said.
William Blanning, Rockwell's director of media relations, said the $3.2 billion deal was structured so it would be tax free.

The vote to sell the unit was in two stages: first, to restructure Rockwell to exclude the defense and aerospace businesses from its operations, and then the issuance of Boeing shares to Rockwell shareholders in return for the businesses.
Beall said the company's debt-free balance sheet should enable it to make strategic acquisitions in the future.
Rockwell also plans to embark on a $1 billion stock repurchase program after the deal.
Boeing shares will be mailed to Rockwell shareholders on December 13, record December 6, a company spokesman said.
Some shareholders said at the special meeting that the deal was not good for Rockwell.
"We have walked away from the business that made us," one shareholder said.
The defense and aerospace unit generated $3.0 billion in revenues and $503 million in operating income in fiscal 1996.

Rockwell's aerospace and defense units had their roots as North American Aviation Inc, building P-51 Mustangs, B-25 Mitchell bombers and the T-6 Texan trainer during World War II. Rockwell helped build the Apollo rocket for the first manned moon landing in 1969 and was prime contractor for the Space Shuttle orbiter.
The defense and aerospace units presently make the B-1B bomber, satellite systems and submarine components and are involved with the United Space Alliance with Lockheed Martin Corp.

"In my judgment, this is a true 'win, win' transaction for Boeing, Rockwell, our customers and employees -- and for you as shareholders," Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Donald Beall said at the meeting.
Analysts have said shrinking defense procurement budgets have pushed many defense contractors to merge or divest weaponry businesses.
Rockwell will now focus on its automation, automotive, avionics and semiconductor systems businesses, Beall said.
